clinicalPearls: Splenic cysts are classified as true (primary) cysts, which possess an epithelial or mesothelial lining, or false (secondary) pseudocysts, which lack a lining and most often follow trauma; congenital epidermoid cysts are the commonest true non-parasitic type

Congenital epidermoid cysts are lined by squamous epithelium and are thought to arise from embryonic inclusion of surface mesothelium within the developing spleen, typically presenting in children and young adults
Most are asymptomatic incidental findings; larger cysts cause left upper quadrant pain or fullness, early satiety, referred left shoulder-tip pain or a palpable mass
The lining epithelium can secrete CA 19-9 and CEA, so serum levels may be raised and then normalise after excision; this is a diagnostic clue and not a marker of malignancy
On imaging a true cyst is a well-defined, thin-walled, non-enhancing fluid lesion, whereas wall calcification and trabeculation favour a pseudocyst, though imaging cannot always separate the two

A parasitic (hydatid) cyst must always be excluded before intervention through exposure history, serology and the search for daughter cysts, because inadvertent spillage can cause anaphylaxis and dissemination

Spleen-preserving surgery such as partial splenectomy, deroofing or decapsulation is preferred over total splenectomy where feasible, to retain immune function and avoid overwhelming post-splenectomy infection
reference.pathophysiology: True congenital splenic (epidermoid) cysts are believed to develop from embryonic entrapment of surface mesothelium within the splenic parenchyma, or from metaplasia of these inclusions, producing a cyst lined by squamous or cuboidal epithelium. This epithelium can elaborate CA 19-9 and CEA, accounting for the raised serum markers seen in some patients. Pseudocysts, in contrast, have no epithelial lining and usually represent the organised, liquefied remnant of a previous haematoma, most often post-traumatic. Progressive accumulation of fluid enlarges the cyst, thins the overlying parenchyma and capsule and predisposes to rupture, intracystic haemorrhage or secondary infection.
additionalDifferentials: Cystic neoplasm such as lymphangioma, haemangioma or cystic metastasis
Pancreatic pseudocyst or cyst indenting the spleen
additionalInvestigations: Ultrasound with Doppler to demonstrate an anechoic, well-defined lesion and assess the wall
Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI to characterise the wall, septa and any enhancement
Serum CA 19-9 and CEA, which may be raised with epithelial cysts
Hydatid serology and indirect haemagglutination where parasitic disease is possible
Full blood count and inflammatory markers if secondary infection or abscess is suspected
Histological examination of the excised specimen to confirm the lining type
redFlags: Acute abdomen or hypovolaemia from cyst rupture or intracystic haemorrhage
Fever and sepsis suggesting secondary infection or abscess formation
Rapid enlargement or solid, septated components raising concern for a neoplasm
A large thin-walled cyst at risk of traumatic rupture
reference.prognosis: Benign congenital splenic cysts carry an excellent prognosis, and spleen-preserving surgery gives durable results with a low recurrence rate, whereas simple aspiration alone commonly recurs. Malignant transformation is very rare.
pitfalls: Interpreting a raised CA 19-9 as evidence of malignancy rather than a benign epithelial cyst
Relying on simple percutaneous aspiration, which frequently leads to recurrence
Missing a parasitic (hydatid) cyst and risking spillage and anaphylaxis at operation
Performing total splenectomy when spleen-preserving surgery would suffice
Neglecting vaccination and infection-prevention advice when splenectomy is unavoidable
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease
management: Conservative observation with interval imaging for small, asymptomatic true cysts or pseudocysts
Exclude a parasitic (hydatid) cyst by exposure history and serology before any intervention, since spillage risks anaphylaxis and dissemination
Spleen-preserving surgery (partial splenectomy, cyst deroofing or fenestration, or marsupialisation) for symptomatic or large cysts to retain splenic immune function
Avoid simple percutaneous aspiration alone as definitive treatment because recurrence is high
Reserve total splenectomy for cysts not amenable to spleen-preserving techniques, with pre-operative immunisation and post-splenectomy infection prophylaxis
Serum CA 19-9 and CEA together with imaging follow-up after excision to document resolution
Histological confirmation of the excised specimen to define the lining and exclude rare malignancy
